title: DoP and camera grammar
purpose: Decide each shot from its visual intent: size, lens, height, move and light, with a reason the audience can feel. Joins between shots use the boundary contract (locked-composition, camera-transition, intentional-cut).
use_cases: Writing a shot as intent first ('we learn she is alone'), then size and lens (wide, 24 mm full-frame equivalent, or a field of view) that deliver it.
Choosing camera height for power: low looks up at a threat, high looks down on someone trapped, eye level is neutral.
Motivating every move: the camera follows an action, reveals information or reflects a change of feeling.

Keeping the 180-degree line across a dialogue, and crossing it only where the audience sees it happen: the camera moves across, a character crosses, or a neutral on-axis shot or a re-establishing wide sits between the two sides. A plain cut across the line is the break.
Lighting with a key-to-fill ratio that fits the mood (low ratio for calm, high for threat); hard or soft light is a separate choice, set by the size of the source.
anti_patterns: A slow push-in on every shot because it 'looks cinematic'; with no motivation it reads as a screensaver.
Lens and size left unspecified, so the model picks a different field of view each shot.
Crossing the line between two continuous shots, flipping who looks left and right.
Chaining the last frame of a shot into a new composition (use camera-transition or intentional-cut instead).
Light direction that changes between shots in one set with no source moving.
Visual attention split: the brightest or sharpest thing in frame is not what the shot is about.

checks.measure: camera.size and camera.lens_mm (full-frame equivalent) or camera.fov are set
a camera move other than static or locked has camera.motivation
EDL boundary contract: axis and hands do not flip across a continuous join
reviewer marks the brightest, sharpest and most saturated area of the key frame
the user reads the shot's intent from the picture
